modules.title: Antiderivatives and the Fundamental Theorem
modules.summary: The theorem that turns an area problem into an algebra problem, and the table of antiderivatives that makes it pay.
concepts: An antiderivative is a family, not a function: if $F' = f$ then so is $F + C$, and the constant is what an initial condition exists to fix
Fundamental Theorem, first half: the accumulation function $A(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ satisfies $A'(x) = f(x)$, so every continuous function has an antiderivative even when no formula for it exists
Fundamental Theorem, second half: $\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$, which is why a closed form beats every quadrature rule in module 1 whenever you can find one
The standard table is the derivative table read backwards, with one exception: $\int x^n\,dx$ is $x^{n+1}/(n+1)$ for every $n$ except $-1$, where it is $\ln|x|$
Linearity, additivity over adjoining subintervals, and the convention $\int_b^a = -\int_a^b$ that keeps the theorem true whichever way the limits run

quiz.title: Antiderivatives and the two halves of the theorem

questions.q: Which of these is an antiderivative of $f(x) = 3x^2$?
questions.why: Differentiate each candidate and keep whichever gives back $3x^2$. That is $x^3 - 7$ — and so would be $x^3$, or $x^3 + 100$, because the constant vanishes under differentiation. That is exactly why an antiderivative is a whole family and why the $+C$ is written. Of the others, $6x$ is the derivative of $3x^2$ rather than its antiderivative, $x^3/3$ differentiates to $x^2$, and $3x^3$ differentiates to $9x^2$.

questions.q: What is $\int_1^e \frac{1}{x}\,dx$?
questions.why: The antiderivative of $1/x$ is $\ln|x|$, so the value is $\ln e - \ln 1 = 1 - 0 = 1$. The power rule $x^{n+1}/(n+1)$ is the one place the table breaks, because at $n = -1$ it divides by zero; $1/x$ has to be handled separately and the logarithm is what fills the gap. The value $e - 1$ is what integrating $e^x$ over the same interval would give.

questions.q: If $A(x) = \int_0^x \sin(t^2)\,dt$, what is $A'(x)$?
questions.why: The first half of the theorem says that differentiating an accumulation function hands back the integrand evaluated at the upper limit, so $A'(x) = \sin(x^2)$ and no integration is required. None is possible either: $\sin(t^2)$ has no elementary antiderivative, which is the whole point — $A$ still exists and is still differentiable. Answers built from $\cos$ come from integrating instead of differentiating, and the extra factor $2x$ belongs to the derivative of $\sin(x^2)$, a different question.

questions.q: Given $\int_0^3 f = 7$ and $\int_0^5 f = 2$, what is $\int_5^3 f$?
questions.why: Additivity gives $\int_0^3 f + \int_3^5 f = \int_0^5 f$, so $\int_3^5 f = 2 - 7 = -5$. The limits asked for run the other way, and reversing them flips the sign, so the value is $+5$. Stopping at $-5$ means the reversal was missed; adding the two given numbers instead of subtracting them gives $9$.

questions.q: Simpson's rule converges as $O(h^4)$ on a smooth integrand. What does the Fundamental Theorem offer that no amount of refinement can?
opts: A faster algorithm for the same approximate answer
The exact value, from one formula evaluated at just the two endpoints
A guarantee that the integrand is continuous
A way to integrate functions that have no antiderivative
questions.why: When an antiderivative $F$ can be found, $F(b) - F(a)$ is the integral exactly, at the cost of two evaluations and no panels at all — a different kind of claim from an error that merely shrinks. It is not universal: most integrands have no elementary antiderivative, and that is precisely where quadrature earns its keep. Continuity is an assumption the theorem needs, not a conclusion it delivers.

modules.title: Substitution: the chain rule run backwards
modules.summary: The technique that rewrites more integrals than all the others together, and the bookkeeping that keeps a definite integral honest.
concepts: Substitution is the chain rule integrated: with $u = g(x)$ and $du = g'(x)\,dx$, $\int f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx = \int f(u)\,du$
The whole skill is spotting a $g'$ already present in the integrand, up to a constant factor you are free to move outside
For a definite integral, push the limits through the substitution to $g(a)$ and $g(b)$ and never change back to $x$
Run the other way, writing $x = h(u)$, the map must be one-to-one on the interval — the requirement behind both trigonometric substitution and the infinite-domain maps of module 2
Symmetry falls out of the same move: over $[-a, a]$ an odd integrand gives $0$ and an even one gives twice the half-integral

questions.q: Which substitution turns $\int 2x\cos(x^2)\,dx$ into something elementary?
questions.why: Take $u = x^2$; then $du = 2x\,dx$ and the $2x$ already sitting in the integrand is consumed exactly, leaving $\int\cos u\,du = \sin(x^2) + C$. The test for a usable substitution is always the same: is the derivative of the inner function already there, up to a constant? Setting $u$ to the whole $\cos(x^2)$ leaves a stray $\sin$ with nothing to cancel it, and $u = 2x$ does not simplify the argument of the cosine at all.

questions.q: Evaluating $\int_0^2 x\,e^{x^2}\,dx$ with $u = x^2$, what does the integral become?
questions.why: $du = 2x\,dx$, so $x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}du$, which supplies the one half. The limits belong to the variable, so they must be pushed through as well: $x = 0$ gives $u = 0$ and $x = 2$ gives $u = 4$. Carrying the old limits over to the new variable is the commonest error here, and it fails quietly — the arithmetic still completes, it just answers a different question.

questions.q: What is $\int_{-1}^{1} x^3\cos x\,dx$?
opts: It cannot be determined without integrating
questions.why: $x^3$ is odd and $\cos x$ is even, so the product is odd, and an odd integrand over an interval symmetric about the origin contributes equal and opposite amounts on the two sides. Doubling the half-integral is the rule for an even integrand, not an odd one. The symmetry argument is a proof rather than an estimate, so nothing needs integrating — and integrating this directly would cost three rounds of parts.

questions.q: $\int \frac{2x + 3}{x^2 + 3x + 7}\,dx$ equals
questions.why: The numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator, so with $u = x^2 + 3x + 7$ the whole thing collapses to $\int du/u = \ln|u| + C$. Recognising that pattern is worth more than any table, because it turns a quotient that looks like a partial-fractions job into one line. The absolute value is carried because in general the denominator can go negative, even though this particular quadratic never does.

questions.q: Substituting $x = h(u)$ rather than $u = g(x)$ carries one extra requirement. What is it?
opts: $h$ must be one-to-one on the interval, so the new limits sweep the old one exactly once
questions.why: Running the substitution backwards means every $x$ in the old interval has to come from exactly one $u$ in the new one. If the map doubles back, part of the interval is covered twice and part not at all. That is why $x = a\sin\theta$ is restricted to $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$, and why module 2 chose $x = a + t/(1-t)$, which increases strictly across $[0, 1)$. The forward direction $u = g(x)$ needs no such condition; it is only the chain rule read backwards.

modules.title: Integration by parts and reduction formulae
modules.summary: The product rule integrated, including the trick of letting an integral appear on both sides of its own equation.
concepts: Integration by parts is the product rule integrated: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$, trading one integral for another you hope is easier
Choose $u$ to be the factor that gets simpler when differentiated — logarithm, then inverse trigonometric, then algebraic, then trigonometric, then exponential
$\int\ln x\,dx$ and $\int\arctan x\,dx$ take $dv = dx$: there is only one factor, and differentiating it is the entire move
$\int e^{ax}\cos(bx)\,dx$ reproduces itself after two rounds, and the answer comes from solving the resulting equation for the unknown integral
A reduction formula expresses $\int\sin^n x\,dx$ through $\int\sin^{n-2}x\,dx$, turning an integral into a recurrence with a base case — the same recurrences that generate Fourier coefficients

quiz.title: Choosing u, and knowing when to stop

questions.q: For $\int x\,e^x\,dx$, which assignment leaves an easier integral behind?
opts: Both of the first two work equally well
questions.why: Differentiating $x$ gives $1$ and removes the algebraic factor entirely, leaving $xe^x - \int e^x\,dx$. Differentiating the exponential instead never simplifies anything, and integrating $x$ into $x^2/2$ makes the remaining integral worse than the original — a reliable sign that the assignment was backwards. Taking the whole product as $u$ simply reproduces the problem you started with.

questions.q: $\int \ln x\,dx$ equals
questions.why: With $u = \ln x$ and $dv = dx$ the formula gives $x\ln x - \int x\cdot\frac{1}{x}\,dx = x\ln x - x + C$. Differentiating the result is the cheapest possible check: $\ln x + 1 - 1 = \ln x$. The answer $\frac{(\ln x)^2}{2}$ belongs to $\int\frac{\ln x}{x}\,dx$, which is a substitution rather than a parts problem, and $1/x$ is the derivative of the integrand instead of its integral.

questions.q: In $\int e^x \sin x\,dx$, two rounds of parts bring the original integral back on the right-hand side. What now?
opts: Conclude that the integral does not exist
Treat the integral as an unknown and solve the equation for it
Abandon parts and use a substitution
questions.why: Two rounds give $I = e^x\sin x - e^x\cos x - I$, an ordinary linear equation whose solution is $I = \frac{1}{2}e^x(\sin x - \cos x) + C$. A third round walks straight back to the starting point, because sine and cosine close under differentiation after two steps. The integral certainly exists — the integrand is continuous everywhere — and no substitution touches it, since neither factor is the derivative of the other.

questions.q: What is a reduction formula for?
opts: Reducing the number of significant figures the answer needs
Expressing an integral through the same integral with a smaller exponent, applied repeatedly down to a base case
Turning a definite integral into an indefinite one
Rewriting a product of two functions as their quotient
questions.why: It converts one integral into a recurrence: $\int\sin^n$ in terms of $\int\sin^{n-2}$, applied until the exponent reaches $0$ or $1$, where the answer is immediate. Structurally it is a recursive function with a base case, and it is how one derivation covers an infinite family of integrals instead of doing $n$ separate ones.

questions.q: What is $\int_0^{\pi} x\sin x\,dx$?
questions.why: With $u = x$ and $dv = \sin x\,dx$ the boundary term $[-x\cos x]_0^{\pi}$ contributes $\pi$, and the leftover $\int_0^{\pi}\cos x\,dx$ contributes nothing, so the value is $\pi$. Both pieces have to be evaluated at the limits; dropping the boundary term is what produces $0$. A quick sanity check settles the sign: the integrand is non-negative across $[0, \pi]$, so a negative answer cannot be right.

modules.title: Trigonometric integrals and trigonometric substitution
modules.summary: The identities that make squared and mixed sinusoids integrable, and the substitutions that clear a square root.
concepts: Power reduction: $\cos^2\theta = \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}$, so a squared sinusoid averages to $\frac{1}{2}$ over a period — the reason an RMS value is the peak divided by $\sqrt{2}$
An odd power of sine or cosine peels off one factor to serve as $du$; an even power has to go through the double-angle identities first
Orthogonality: over a full period $\int\sin(mx)\sin(nx)$ and $\int\sin(mx)\cos(nx)$ vanish unless the frequencies match, which is what every Fourier coefficient formula rests on
The three substitutions: $x = a\sin\theta$ for $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$, $x = a\tan\theta$ for $\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}$, $x = a\sec\theta$ for $\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}$
Complete the square first to reach one of those three forms, and come back through a right triangle rather than through nested inverse functions

questions.q: What is the average value of $\sin^2(\omega t)$ over one full period?
questions.why: Rewrite it as $\frac{1 - \cos 2\omega t}{2}$. The cosine completes whole cycles over a period and averages to nothing, leaving $\frac{1}{2}$. Taking the square root of that mean is what produces the RMS value, so $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ is the RMS of the sinusoid rather than the mean of its square; and $0$ is the average of the raw $\sin$, not of $\sin^2$, which is never negative.

questions.q: What is $\int_0^{2\pi}\sin(3x)\cos(5x)\,dx$?
questions.why: A product-to-sum identity turns it into $\frac{1}{2}\int[\sin(8x) - \sin(2x)]\,dx$, and both sinusoids complete a whole number of cycles across $[0, 2\pi]$, so both integrate to nothing. Sines and cosines at integer multiples of one frequency are orthogonal in exactly this sense, which is what lets a Fourier coefficient be extracted by multiplying the signal by one harmonic and integrating: every other harmonic contributes zero. The value $\pi$ is what appears when the frequencies do match and the two factors are the same kind of function.

questions.q: What is the right first move for $\int\sin^3 x\cos^2 x\,dx$?
opts: Write $\sin^3 x = (1 - \cos^2 x)\sin x$ and substitute $u = \cos x$
Apply the double-angle identity to both factors
questions.why: The sine carries an odd power, so one factor of $\sin x$ can be set aside to become $du$ for $u = \cos x$, and the even remainder $\sin^2 x$ converts to $1 - \cos^2 x$ by the Pythagorean identity. What is left is a polynomial in $u$. Substituting $u = \sin x$ fails because $du = \cos x\,dx$ needs an odd power of cosine and this one is even. Double-angle identities are the tool when both powers are even, and they cost considerably more work.

questions.q: Which substitution clears the root in $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{9 + x^2}}$?
questions.why: With $x = 3\tan\theta$, $9 + x^2 = 9(1 + \tan^2\theta) = 9\sec^2\theta$, and the square root comes out as $3\sec\theta$ with no root left. The sine substitution is built for $a^2 - x^2$ and here would leave $9 + 9\sin^2\theta$, which factors into nothing useful. A plain $u = 9 + x^2$ fails for a different reason: $du = 2x\,dx$ and there is no $x$ in the numerator to supply it.

questions.q: What should you do to $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 - 6x + 13}}$ before choosing a substitution?
opts: Factor the quadratic into linear terms
questions.why: Completing the square turns the quadratic into $(x-3)^2 + 4$, which is the $a^2 + u^2$ pattern with $u = x - 3$ and $a = 2$, so $u = 2\tan\theta$ finishes the job. Factoring into real linear terms is impossible — the discriminant $36 - 52$ is negative — and partial fractions applies to rational functions, not to something sitting under a square root.

modules.title: Rational functions and partial fractions
modules.summary: Breaking a quotient of polynomials into pieces small enough that each one is a logarithm or an arctangent.
concepts: Divide first: the decomposition only exists once the numerator's degree is below the denominator's, so a polynomial long division comes before anything else
Factor the denominator; each distinct linear factor $(x - r)$ contributes one term $A/(x - r)$, and the cover-up method reads $A$ off in a single step
A repeated factor $(x - r)^m$ needs one term for every power from $1$ to $m$, not only the highest
An irreducible quadratic contributes $(Ax + B)/(x^2 + bx + c)$, which after completing the square splits into a logarithm plus an arctangent
This is the same algebra that splits a transfer function into its poles before an inverse transform, so the decompositions written here reappear unchanged in later courses

questions.q: What has to happen before $\frac{x^3}{x^2 - 1}$ can be decomposed into partial fractions?
opts: Nothing — it is already in a decomposable form
A polynomial long division, because the numerator's degree is not below the denominator's
Completing the square in the denominator
questions.why: Degree three over degree two is improper, and no sum of terms shaped like $A/(x - 1)$ can ever produce the leading $x$ that division pulls out. Dividing gives $x + \frac{x}{x^2 - 1}$, and only the remainder gets decomposed. Skipping the division produces a system of equations with no solution, which at least fails loudly rather than quietly.

questions.q: In $\frac{5}{(x-1)(x+4)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x+4}$, what is the numerator $A$?
questions.why: Multiply both sides by $(x - 1)$ and set $x = 1$: the other term is annihilated by its own factor and what remains is $5/(1 + 4) = 1$. That is the cover-up method — hide the factor you are solving for and substitute its root into everything else. Expanding and matching coefficients reaches the same number through several more lines of algebra and several more chances to slip.

questions.q: Which is the correct form for $\frac{1}{x(x-2)^2}$?
questions.why: A factor repeated twice needs a term at each power up to the repeat, so both $\frac{B}{x-2}$ and $\frac{C}{(x-2)^2}$ have to appear; leaving out the first-power term makes the system unsolvable in general. A linear numerator $Bx + C$ belongs over an irreducible quadratic, and $(x-2)^2$ is not irreducible — it is a linear factor squared.

questions.q: $\int\frac{dx}{x^2 + 4}$ equals
questions.why: The standard form is $\int\frac{dx}{x^2 + a^2} = \frac{1}{a}\arctan\frac{x}{a} + C$, here with $a = 2$, so both the $\frac{1}{2}$ outside and the $\frac{x}{2}$ inside are needed. A logarithm appears only when the numerator is a multiple of $2x$, the derivative of the denominator, which it is not. A general $(Ax + B)$ numerator over an irreducible quadratic splits into one piece of each kind, one logarithm and one arctangent.

questions.q: Which of these is genuinely a partial-fractions problem rather than a substitution?
questions.why: A proper rational function whose denominator factors into distinct linear pieces is exactly what the method exists for. By contrast $\int\frac{2x}{x^2+1}\,dx$ carries the derivative of its own denominator on top and is a one-line logarithm; $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ is the standard arcsine form; and $\int x\sqrt{x^2+1}\,dx$ yields to $u = x^2 + 1$. Reaching for partial fractions before checking for an $f'/f$ pattern is a good way to turn one line into a page.

modules.title: Applications of the definite integral
modules.summary: Slice the quantity, approximate one slice by something you can already measure, and let the slice width go to zero.
concepts: Area between two curves is $\int(\text{upper} - \text{lower})\,dx$, split at every crossing, because a signed integral would cancel what you meant to add
Volumes of revolution: a disk or washer when the slice is perpendicular to the axis, a cylindrical shell $2\pi x f(x)\,dx$ when it runs parallel to it
Arc length $\int\sqrt{1 + f'(x)^2}\,dx$ and the surface of revolution $\int 2\pi f(x)\sqrt{1 + f'(x)^2}\,dx$ come from the same slice, measured two different ways

Average value $\bar f = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f$, attained somewhere by the mean value theorem for integrals; the root mean square $\sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T f^2}$ is the average engineering quotes instead
Work is $\int F\,dx$ and stored energy is $\int v\,i\,dt$: whenever a product of two quantities is only valid for an instant, the total is an integral and not a multiplication

questions.q: What is the area of the region between $y = x$ and $y = x^2$ for $0 \le x \le 1$?
questions.why: On $[0, 1]$ the line lies above the parabola, so the area is $\int_0^1 (x - x^2)\,dx = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{6}$. Integrating the two curves separately and adding gives $\frac{5}{6}$, which is the area under both rather than between them. Subtracting the other way round gives $-\frac{1}{6}$, and a negative area is the signal that the upper curve was misidentified.

questions.q: Rotating the region under $y = f(x)$ from $x = a$ to $x = b$ about the $y$-axis, which integral is the shell method?
questions.why: A shell at radius $x$ has circumference $2\pi x$, height $f(x)$ and thickness $dx$, so its volume is $2\pi x f(x)\,dx$. The form $\pi f(x)^2$ is the disk method, which is correct for rotation about the $x$-axis and answers a different question here. Choosing between them is choosing the direction of the slice, and shells usually win when they let you keep the variable you already have a formula in.

questions.q: In the arc length formula $\int_a^b\sqrt{1 + f'(x)^2}\,dx$, where does the $1$ come from?
opts: The horizontal leg $dx$ of the small right triangle whose hypotenuse is the arc
The requirement that a length be positive
The average value of $f$ over the interval
questions.why: A short piece of curve is the hypotenuse of a triangle with legs $dx$ and $dy$, so its length is $\sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2}$, and factoring $dx$ out leaves $\sqrt{1 + (dy/dx)^2}\,dx$. The $1$ is the horizontal leg, squared. Seeing that also explains why arc-length integrands are so often ugly: a square root of a polynomial rarely has an elementary antiderivative, which is exactly when the adaptive quadrature of module 2 gets used in earnest.

questions.q: A voltage $v(t) = V\sin(\omega t)$ averages to zero over a full cycle. Why is its RMS value not zero as well?
opts: Because the RMS is taken over half a cycle only
Because squaring first makes every contribution non-negative, so nothing cancels
Because the RMS uses the absolute value of the integral
Because the average is only zero for an ideal source
questions.why: RMS squares before it averages, and a square is never negative, so the negative half-cycle contributes just as much as the positive one; the square root at the end returns the result to the original units. That is precisely the quantity that sets the heating in a resistor, because power goes as $v^2$ and not as $v$. Nothing about it involves halving the interval, and the mean of the raw sinusoid really is zero — which is why the plain mean is the wrong average for this job.

questions.q: A spring obeying $F(x) = kx$ is stretched from $0$ to $L$. How much work is done?
questions.why: Force times distance only holds while the force is constant, so the total is $\int_0^L kx\,dx = \frac{1}{2}kL^2$. Multiplying the final force $kL$ by the distance $L$ gives $kL^2$, twice the truth, because it charges the whole journey at the highest force. The same argument in a different costume produces $\frac{1}{2}CV^2$ for a charged capacitor and $\frac{1}{2}LI^2$ for an inductor.

modules.title: Power series as functions
modules.summary: Once a function is a series it can be substituted into, differentiated and integrated like a polynomial — which is how the awkward integrals get done.
concepts: The geometric series $\frac{1}{1-x} = \sum_{n \ge 0} x^n$ for $|x| < 1$ is the one series that costs no differentiation at all, and most others are built from it
Substituting into and multiplying known series beats computing $n$ derivatives: $\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ is the geometric series evaluated at $-x^2$, in one line
Inside the radius of convergence a power series may be differentiated and integrated term by term, and the radius survives the operation — which turns geometric series into $\ln(1+x)$ and $\arctan x$
The binomial series extends $(1+x)^k$ to every real exponent $k$, and terminates into the ordinary binomial theorem exactly when $k$ is a non-negative integer

An integrand with no elementary antiderivative — $e^{-x^2}$, or $\frac{\sin x}{x}$ — is integrated by expanding it and integrating term by term, with the truncation sized by module 3's remainder bound

questions.q: For which $x$ does $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x^n$ converge, and to what?
questions.why: The partial sum is $\frac{1 - x^{n+1}}{1 - x}$, and $x^{n+1} \to 0$ exactly when $|x| < 1$. Outside that the terms do not even tend to zero, so the $n$th-term test from module 4 rules convergence out before anything subtler is needed. Checking $x = \frac{1}{2}$, where the series sums to $2$, settles the sign in the denominator.

questions.q: Using the geometric series, the expansion of $\frac{1}{1 + x^2}$ begins
questions.why: Put $-x^2$ where the geometric series has its variable: $\frac{1}{1 - (-x^2)} = 1 + (-x^2) + (-x^2)^2 + \cdots = 1 - x^2 + x^4 - \cdots$. No derivatives are computed at any point. The all-plus version expands $\frac{1}{1 - x^2}$ instead, the alternating series in odd powers of $x$ is $\arctan x$, which is what you get after integrating this one term by term, and $1 - x + x^2 - \cdots$ expands $\frac{1}{1+x}$.

questions.q: Integrating $1 - t^2 + t^4 - \cdots$ term by term from $0$ to $x$ gives
questions.why: Term by term the integral is $x - \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{x^5}{5} - \cdots$, and since the integrand sums to $\frac{1}{1 + t^2}$, the result is $\arctan x$. Putting $x = 1$ turns that into the classical $\pi/4$ series, which converges so slowly that it is a good reminder that a series being correct and a series being useful are separate claims. The logarithm comes from integrating the geometric series in $-t$ rather than in $-t^2$.

questions.q: When is term-by-term differentiation and integration of a power series valid?
opts: Only for series with finitely many terms
Strictly inside the radius of convergence, where the radius is unchanged by the operation
Only when every coefficient is positive
questions.why: Inside the radius the convergence is good enough — uniform on any closed subinterval — that both operations pass through the sum, and the differentiated and integrated series have the same radius as the original. The endpoints are the exception and must be checked separately, since convergence there can be gained or lost. Outside the radius there is nothing to differentiate, because the series represents no function at all.

questions.q: $\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx$ has no elementary antiderivative. What is the series route to a value?
opts: Give up on calculus and read the answer from a table
Substitute $-x^2$ into the exponential series, integrate term by term, and truncate with a remainder bound
Split the integrand into partial fractions
questions.why: $e^{-x^2} = \sum\frac{(-x^2)^n}{n!}$ integrates term by term to $\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{n!\,(2n+1)}$, an alternating series whose truncation error is bounded by the first term left out. So the answer arrives with an error bar, exactly as the quadrature of module 2 does, but reached from the other side. Partial fractions needs a rational integrand and there is nothing rational here.

capstone.title: Capstone — quadrature and series library with error guarantees
capstone.brief:
Fold the four labs into one library. `quadlib.py` holds every routine and is
what the checks import; `main.py` is a demo that integrates a handful of
awkward integrals, sums a series and prints an error report.

Every numerical routine returns the same record, so callers never have to guess
what a bare float means.

## `Result`

A dataclass with three fields, in this order:

- `value` — the number
- `error` — the routine's own estimate of how wrong it might be
- `evaluations` — how many times the integrand or term was called

## Integration

- `simpson(f, a, b, n)` — composite Simpson on `n` even panels; `ValueError`
  for odd `n` or `n < 2`. Returns a plain float, not a `Result`.
- `adaptive(f, a, b, tol, max_depth=30)` — the recursive Simpson of lab 2,
  returning a `Result`. `error` is the sum of `abs(delta) / 15` over the
  accepted panels; `evaluations` counts every call made to `f`. An empty
  interval gives `Result(0.0, 0.0, 0)`; a reversed one negates `value` only.
- `integrate(f, a, b, tol=1e-9)` — the front door. `a` or `b` may be
  `math.inf` / `-math.inf`, handled by the substitutions from lab 2 (split the
  doubly infinite case at 0 and give each half `tol / 2`). `tol <= 0` and any
  NaN bound raise `ValueError`.

## Series

- `taylor_coefficients(kind, n)`, `taylor_eval(coeffs, x)`,
  `taylor_bound(kind, x, n)` — exactly as in lab 3.
- `series_sum(term, tail_integral, tol, max_terms=200000)` — lab 4's
  `estimate_sum`, returning a `Result` whose `evaluations` is the number of
  terms used.

## Reporting

`error_report(entries)` takes a list of `(name, result, exact_or_None)` and
returns a string of exactly `len(entries) + 2` lines:

1. a header line beginning with `quantity`
2. one line per entry, starting with `name`, containing the value, the claimed
   bound and — when `exact` is given — the actual error
3. a final line starting with `TOTAL EVALUATIONS` and ending with the summed
   evaluation count

## Suggested order

`Result` and `simpson`, then `adaptive` with its counter, then `integrate`'s
dispatch on infinite bounds, then the series half, and `error_report` last.
deliverables: `quadlib.py` — the whole library, importable with no output and no side effects
`main.py` — a demo integrating a proper, an infinite and an oscillatory integral, then summing a series
A `Result` record carrying value, error estimate and evaluation count from every routine
`integrate` dispatching correctly on finite, semi-infinite and doubly infinite domains
`series_sum` returning an integral-test bracket that provably contains the true sum
`error_report` producing a table a marker can read without running anything
constraints: Standard library only; `math` and `dataclasses` are all you need
`quadlib.py` must define names only — importing it must print nothing
No global mutable state: two concurrent integrations must not share an evaluation counter
Every public routine validates its arguments and raises `ValueError` rather than returning nonsense
The whole demo must finish in well under a second

rubric.evidence: All automated checks pass, including the infinite-domain, reversed-interval and empty-interval cases.
Reported error estimates actually bound the observed error on the tested integrals, and tightening tol tightens the answer.
Non-positive tolerances, odd Simpson panel counts and NaN bounds all raise ValueError.
integrate dispatches onto shared helpers rather than duplicating the refinement loop, and the counter is per-call.
Docstrings on every public routine, no dead code, no debug prints left in quadlib.py.

import math
from quadlib import integrate, series_sum, error_report

rows = [
    ("exp on [0,1]", integrate(math.exp, 0.0, 1.0, 1e-10), math.e - 1.0),
    ("exp(-x) to inf", integrate(lambda x: math.exp(-x), 0.0, math.inf, 1e-10), 1.0),
    ("gaussian", integrate(lambda x: math.exp(-x * x), -math.inf, math.inf, 1e-10), math.sqrt(math.pi)),
    ("basel series", series_sum(lambda k: 1.0 / k ** 2, lambda x: 1.0 / x, 1e-8), math.pi ** 2 / 6.0),
]

print(error_report(rows))

runge = integrate(lambda x: 1.0 / (1.0 + 25.0 * x * x), -1.0, 1.0, 1e-10)
print("Runge integral:", runge.value, "in", runge.evaluations, "evaluations")

hints: Wrap the integrand in a small closure that increments a list-of-one counter; returning `(wrapped, box)` from a helper keeps the state local to one call.
Have `_refine` return the pair `(value, error)` and add the two halves' errors on the way back up — that is the whole error budget.

`integrate` is a dispatch table, not an algorithm: empty interval, reversed interval, both infinite, upper infinite, lower infinite, otherwise `adaptive`. Reflect the lower-infinite case with `lambda x: f(-x)` and negated bounds.
Merge sub-results with one helper that sums values, sums errors and sums evaluation counts, so every branch of `integrate` returns the same shape.

tests.name: Result carries value, error and evaluations
tests.code:
import math as _m
from quadlib import Result, adaptive
_r = Result(1.5, 1e-9, 42)
assert (_r.value, _r.error, _r.evaluations) == (1.5, 1e-9, 42), f"Result fields came back as {_r!r}"
_got = adaptive(_m.sin, 0.0, _m.pi, 1e-10)
assert isinstance(_got, Result), f"adaptive returned {type(_got).__name__}, expected Result"
assert abs(_got.value - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"adaptive(sin, 0, pi) gave {_got.value!r}, expected 2.0"
assert _got.evaluations > 0, "adaptive must count its integrand calls"

tests.name: Composite Simpson
tests.code:
import math as _m
from quadlib import simpson
_got = simpson(lambda x: x ** 3, 0.0, 1.0, 2)
assert abs(_got - 0.25) < 1e-14, f"simpson(x^3, 0, 1, 2) gave {_got!r}, expected 0.25"
_got = simpson(_m.exp, 0.0, 1.0, 100)
assert abs(_got - (_m.e - 1.0)) < 1e-9, f"simpson(exp, 0, 1, 100) gave {_got!r}"
for _bad in (1, 3, 0, -2):
    try:
        simpson(_m.sin, 0.0, 1.0, _bad)
        assert False, f"simpson with n={_bad} should raise ValueError"
    except ValueError:
        pass

import math as _m
from quadlib import adaptive
for _name, _f, _a, _b, _want in [("sin", _m.sin, 0.0, _m.pi, 2.0),
                                 ("exp", _m.exp, 0.0, 1.0, _m.e - 1.0),
                                 ("runge", lambda x: 1.0 / (1.0 + 25.0 * x * x), -1.0, 1.0,
                                  2.0 * _m.atan(5.0) / 5.0)]:
    _r = adaptive(_f, _a, _b, 1e-10)
    assert abs(_r.value - _want) < 1e-9, f"adaptive on {_name} gave {_r.value!r}, expected {_want!r}"
    assert abs(_r.value - _want) <= _r.error + 1e-12, \
        f"On {_name} the actual error beat the claimed bound {_r.error!r}"

_r = adaptive(_m.sin, 2.0, 2.0, 1e-9)

_f = adaptive(_m.sin, 0.0, _m.pi, 1e-10)
_b = adaptive(_m.sin, _m.pi, 0.0, 1e-10)

tests.name: Tightening the tolerance tightens the answer
tests.code:
import math as _m
from quadlib import integrate
_exact = _m.e - 1.0
_loose = integrate(_m.exp, 0.0, 1.0, 1e-3)
_tight = integrate(_m.exp, 0.0, 1.0, 1e-12)
assert abs(_loose.value - _exact) < 1e-3, f"tol=1e-3 left an error of {abs(_loose.value - _exact)!r}"
assert abs(_tight.value - _exact) < 1e-11, f"tol=1e-12 left an error of {abs(_tight.value - _exact)!r}"
assert _tight.evaluations > _loose.evaluations, \
    f"A tighter tolerance used {_tight.evaluations} evaluations vs {_loose.evaluations} — it should cost more"

import math as _m
from quadlib import taylor_coefficients, taylor_eval, taylor_bound
assert taylor_coefficients("exp", 3) == [1.0, 1.0, 0.5, 1.0 / 6.0], \
    f"Got {taylor_coefficients('exp', 3)!r}"
assert taylor_coefficients("cos", 4)[1] == 0.0 and abs(taylor_coefficients("cos", 4)[2] + 0.5) < 1e-15, \
    f"cos coefficients came back as {taylor_coefficients('cos', 4)!r}"
_got = taylor_eval(taylor_coefficients("sin", 15), 0.7)
assert abs(_got - _m.sin(0.7)) < 1e-12, f"sin series at 0.7 gave {_got!r}, expected {_m.sin(0.7)!r}"
assert abs(taylor_bound("sin", 0.5, 3) - 0.5 ** 4 / 24.0) < 1e-18, \
    f"taylor_bound('sin', 0.5, 3) gave {taylor_bound('sin', 0.5, 3)!r}"
for _kind, _fn in [("exp", _m.exp), ("cos", _m.cos)]:
    for _x in (-1.5, 0.4, 2.0):
        _err = abs(taylor_eval(taylor_coefficients(_kind, 8), _x) - _fn(_x))
